@graph.biography:
Koormundum (Ida Edwards) was born in Darwin Hospital on 1st August 1926 to Harry and Poordjetpudjen (Margaret Edwards). Poordjetpudjen was the only daughter of Kungarakan matriarch, Ulynudubbu (Lucy), and Irishman Stephen McGuiness who immigrated to Australia as a young man in his early twenties. Lucy and Stephen had four other children, Barney, John (Jack), Val and Joe McGuinness, who are the forefathers of many Kungarakan. 

As the only girl in their clan, prior to his death in 1917, Stephen arranged for his friend, Harry Edwards to marry Poorjetpudjen in 1919. This was primarily to avoid her fate under the laws that governed the lives of Aboriginal people at that time. The first few years of Ida’s life was spent in a corrugated iron home in Woods Street, Darwin, then in a humpy at Darwin River where Harry worked a family tin mine named “The Lucy Claim”. Some of Koormundum first and fondest memories were of her Grannie, Lucy from whom she learned Kungarakan language as a child. Due to the chronic ill-health of her father Harry, he and his family moved south to Melbourne. Her father’s passing a few years later left Koormundum and her mother stranded from their much-loved country and family in the North. 

Koormundum continued and finished her education in Melbourne, graduating from Stotts Business College at the age of 19 with a Diploma in Business. She was employed as bookkeeper and typist. In her spare time she played violin in a string quartet as and was a member of the church choir. In 1952, Ida married a man she’d met at choir, Graham Bishop. Graham’s job as a school teacher took them all over the country and to territories like Christmas Island and the ACT. It was in Canberra when she applied to the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies for a grant to help fund her ongoing and continued work on Kungarakan language. For the next 30 years’ she would document the language and history of her Kungarakan people and self-publish ngun Koongurrukun: Speak Koongurrukun, in 2000. 

Whilst many years were spent moving for work and raising six children, Koormundum never lost sight of her identity and role as a Kungarakan woman. Through the years, she kept in regular contact with her NT-based family and, even after her book was published, continued to research and advocate for Kungarakan people. She attended and gave evidence to the Finniss River Land Claim hearings in the early 1980s. She prepared vital evidence, maps and genealogies with her Elders and cousins, ultimately Kungarakan winning their case with their land restored them. 

Ida was an avid reader and writer. She wrote poetry and short stories. Her numerous notebooks record details anyone else may have missed or ignored. Ida’s love of words and language made her a great communicator, known to strike up conversations with strangers just to have a chat, regardless of where she happened to be. It didn’t seem to matter that she couldn’t speak their language, people always seemed to understand her. These traits made her the ideal language champion. 

Ida’s life work is her legacy, she did what was within her power to do, to keep Kungurrukun language alive. 

This work was dedicated to her mother Poordjetpudjen in keeping her promise to preserve Koongurrukun language. This enormous work is also Koormundum’s ngirrwut, the transferring of her knowledge, faithfully to all Koongurrukun to be understood from its own cultural basis and the very essence of Koongurrukun identity. Sadly, Koormundum passed away on 20th April 2014 her identity and her work gained us back our language. Her land rose up through surviving speakers so that she could hear it once more and return it to the people so it may speak through them once again. 

 Prepared by her children, Anthony, Katherine, Helen, Barbara, Andrew and Meg.

@graph.language_description:
Ungarinyin is the name of the people and their language and is known as heavy pronunciation. Ngarinyin is also the people and their language and is known as light pronunciation.  When people are speaking they use Ungarinyin to talk about themselves and their relationship to their environment.

Ngarinyin is very closely related to Wurla and they are linked together in the Native Title Area. There are more than 62 clan estates in Wanjina-Wilinggin-Wunggurr Native Title claim, which was awarded in 2004.

Ngarinyin includes the dialects: Wilawila, Wolyamidi, Guwidj, Wurla, Ola, Walar, Worla, Wula, Wuladja, Wuladjangari.

Ngarinyin country is generally associated with the western half of the Kimberley Plateau. These are the Ngarinyin place names travelling roughly west to east. Gawulara (Napier Range), Walarra (New Mount Hart), Gambarrambal (Old Mount Hart), Dalandi (Silent Grove), Iminji (Imintji), Jilariba (Munja), Malbirri (Pantijan), Gubungarri (Mount Barnett), Waa (New Mount Elizabeth), Nyangudunda (Old Mount Elizabeth), Dodnan (Dodnun), Nyalanggunda (Gibb River Homestead), Umalagurdunda (Old Beverley Springs), Balamandarra (Gibb River), Darlngga (Drysdale River), Man.gurerri (Doongan), Marranbabidi (PrapPrap), Munuru (King Edward River Crossing), Gurrunggu (Mount House Homestead), Garrenji (Karunjie), Theda Station, Malambu  (El Questro), Marion Downs.

Alan Rumsey with David Mowaljarlai† developed the Ngarinyin orthography used by the Mowanjum Language Project and is a modified version of practical orthography developed by linguist Barry Blake.

Ngarinyin spellings include: Ungarinyin, Ngarinjin, Ungarinjin, Narrinyind.

Marri Amu includes the coastal strip from just south of Nganthiwudi (Cape Scott) continuing south to Anggileni (Cape Dombey). To the north is Mendheyangal country, to the east is Marrithiyel country and to the south is Marri Tjevin country (Marett et al. 2013).
Marri Amu and Marri Tjevin are mutually intelligible and are classified by linguists as dialects of the same language. @graph.language_description:
Wunambal Gaambera is spoken in the most north-westerly part of the Kimberley region. Wunambal and Gaambera are ‘very closely related’, with very little difference in pronunciation and some different words. Karadada et al. (2011) explains 'It is possible that there were some differences in the past, but in recent times these differences have faded'.

According to McGregor (1993) Wunambal and Gaambera are also closely related to the other north Kimberley languages, Kwini, Miwa and Yiiji and more distantly related to Worlaja, Ngarinyin and Worrorra.

The Wunambal Gaambera people received their Native Title determination – Wanjina Wunggurr Uunguu in 2011 (Karadada et al. 2011) and now work together as one group with their country listed as the Uunguu Indigenous Protection Area. Their country covers 2.5 million hectares of land and sea in the north Kimberley region of Australia.

Country associated with Wunambal Gaambera (Karadada et al. 2011) extends from north of the Prince Regent River taking in Ngauwudu (Mitchell Plateau), Scott’s Strait and Gibulde (Cape Voltaire), and some inland countries. Some ‘clans’ also exploited the resources of the adjoining small islands, especially Wuuyurru (Bigge Island), Prudhoe Island, Corneille Island and Cassini islands although, apart from Wuyurru, these islands were not permanently inhabited. Other Wunambal Gaambera places are Punamii Uunpuu (Mitchell Falls), Kandiwal, Wung-gaarindjii (Katers Island), Jalandal, Banjal (Vansittart Bay), Garmbemirri, Wapenbe, Mungulalu (Anjo Peninsula) and Wargul Wargul (Bougainville Peninsula).

 The Wunambal Gaambera orthography used for the Mowanjum Language Project was developed by Therese Carr and Wilfred Goonack†. The orthography has been updated from the pronunciation guide in Uunguu Plants and Animals: Aboriginal biological knowledge from Wunambal Gaambera Country in the north-west Kimberley.

 

Wunambal spellings include: Wunumbal, Wunabal, Wunambul, Wunumbul, Wonambul, Unambal, Woonambal, Wunambullu, Wunumabal, Woonambal.

Gaambera spellings include: Gambera, Gamberre, Gambre.

@graph.language_description:
According to the Damimangari Aboriginal Corporation (2012) the Worrorra language has eight clan groups: Larrinyuwai, Arrbarlandi, Uminda, Unggarrang, Yawijabay, Uurnbun, Wurnbangkurwai and Ornnorrongoy, and together they are referred as the Dambimangari; Saltwater people. The Dambimangari people were awarded their Native Title Determination in 2011.

As explained in the Damimangari Healthy Country Plan (2012), Worrorra speaking families lived traditionally on and near the north-west Kimberley coast between “Ungarrang at the bottom of Kimbolton to Marlundum in the Prince Regent area”. Clendon (2014, p.2) in collaboration with Worrorran language custodians, confirms that “in the south, Worrorra country extended inland some 40 kilometres from the coast, and in the north, roughly some 60 kilometres inland, and 50 or so kilometres up the Malanduma (Prince Regent River Region), from where it empties into the St. George Basin. This region includes the lower and middle reaches of Malanduma (Prince Regent River Region), Ngarlangkarnanya (St. George Basin) Ngayangkarnanya (Mt. Trafalgar) and Nubungarri (Mt. Waterloo). It includes the George Water and Arn Nowngoy (Glenelg River) and Iledda (Walcott Inlet). On the coast Worrorra country includes Wurroolgu (Augustus Island) as well as many other offshore islands, and Yawijaba (Montgomery Islands and reefs)”.

The Worrorra orthography that has been used throughout the Mowanjum Language Project is based on the orthography developed by Mark Clendon with Sam Umbagai†, Amy Peters†, Daisy Utermorrah†, Patsy Lulpunda† and Heather Umbagai†, however there have been several changes to the orthography over the last five years as requested by senior Worrorra speakers.

Worrorra spellings include: Worora, Worrora, Wororra, Wurara, Worara, Woddodda

@graph.language_description:
Pumbah (footprints or walking tracks) encompass many travelling and trading routes across and through lok Koongurrukun (Koongurrukun country). There exists a loop that starts with wulwul jirruk, (Tumbling Waters) with its effervescent springs, mibi cober koormandum, (underground eyes of water) to embrace Luniook (Berry Springs) then across Panawulk at (Blackmore) and Nungulukoo (Finniss) Rivers and the important sites  in Purlugutj ( Litchfield National Park). Pumbah winds its way across and through the interior to take many pumbah to Annrukulpum (Rum Jungle) and into Ulmoolmi (Batchelor). While there are coastal pumbah the central location is Kurrinju.  The north-eastern boundary includes Lanji  (Darwin River), Tjetiring shared with the  Warai peoples near the area now known as Manton Dam. The pumbah networks travel south down through to Amulgul (Adelaide River. Helen Bishop 2017

Tindale: Koongurrukun Estate: Northeast of Mount Litchfield on midwaters of Reynolds River and on Adelaide River headwaters; an inland tribe extending to the western side of the Tabletop Range divide; northeast to vicinity of Rum Jungle and Batchelor.  http://archives.samuseum.sa.gov.au/tindaletribes/kungarakan.htm

@graph.biography: Jeff Hardwick was born in Griffith NSW in 1952 and has had a life long love of nature. Jeff has a huge fascination and admiration for Aboriginal people and how they lived in the bush and their language, song, art and dancing. Jeff is a qualified teacher and has lectured in Conservation and Land Management. After 35 years Jeff returned to Wadeye (Port Keats) to continue the work he started in the 1970s to document material culture and support the recording of endangered languages at Wadeye. He currently works for Batchelor Institute as a Project Officer in the Wadeye Endangered Languages Project supporting documentation and revival of knowledge and skills with the Wadeye Community.

@graph.biography: Maree has worked in Aboriginal education for the past 35 years with much of this time being spent working with people from rural and remote communities in the Northern Territory. Her experiences include, primary teaching, higher education in both-ways Aboriginal remote teacher education, bilingual education, ESL, information technology in education and publishing Aboriginal languages and teaching and learning resources. Maree is currently the Manager of Batchelor Press, Co Director of the Centre for Australian Languages and Linguistics and Project Manager for Wadeye and Mowanjum language project teams supporting language maintenance, revival and education.

@graph.biography: Killinang was born at Overn Station. Sometimes his family came to the Old Mission at Werntek Nganinyi to visit for rations and then they would go back to Wudipuli and Nama. After a while they stopped at the mission and Killinang went to school with his brothers. Killinang became a stockman working on stations at Kulchil, Tipperary, Litchfield and Wangi. Then he went back to Wadeye (Port Keats) for a while, but soon left to work at Victoria River Downs Campfield Station. He was mustering, fencing, and doing all the work of a stockman. He came back to Wadeye and got married. He also worked in gardens and in building trades. Killinang is famous for his dancing and for playing the didgeridoo. He travelled to Kununurra, Turkey Creek, Fitzroy Crossing and Derby as a dancer for ceremonies. Killinang was happy working at the language centre and taking part in ceremonies. He enjoyed hunting at Nama and sometimes at Kidenu or Nganbe.

@graph.biography: Lungung Johnny Nama was born at Daly River but grew up at Dirrangara. His grandfather Tchinburrur was boss for Ma Muyil people. Before the war when he was a little boy he went to Old Mission (Werntek Nganinyi) with all his family, mother, father and grandfather. The family then went back to Dirrangara, but after a while they returned to Old Mission for tobacco and rations like sugar. They would travel back and forth from their country to Old Mission for tobacco and rations. During the war Lungung’s family decided to go back and stay at Old Mission and Lungung became a timber man, cutting stringy bark trees. He also travelled to Tipperary and Litchfield as a timber man, Lungung was married to Joan Pupuli and they had six children.

@graph.biography: His father was going for kangaroo when he was a little boy, he went with his father. They went hunting to Mangure (Gibb River) downstream. Something about dreamtime there is a big Wadjina painting there Ngawera is the Wadjina at Donkey Creek. (Donkey creek that is their country) They walked and they walked, there were lots of watermelon. The station white-fellas he busted the watermelon, he opened it up and put poison for the dingo on the watermelon. His father found one watermelon already smashed and he ate the watermelon, his father died. Well he didn’t eat the watermelon and there he was a little fella maybe almost a teenager maybe 8-9yrs old. He walked back to Gibb Station and one woman found him walking on the airstrip, they asked where is your father and he said, no he is finished now. So he stayed there at Gibb River Stations and grew up to be a stockman.

@graph.biography: Larri Rex Munar was born at Nganthamurri. He lived with his parents out in the bush. He would go hunting with his father and his father would tell him stories about their country. Larri worked as a stockman with Brother Quinn around Kura Chipmam, Kura Yipi, Kulchil and Palumpa Station. Later he came back to Wadeye (Port Keats) and got married to May Pupil. They had five children. Larri was happy working at the Wadeye Aboriginal Languages Centre and enjoyed taking the family to Nama and Wudipuli for bush holidays.

@graph.biography: Maxie is the son of Mawanyngu Jeanie Jongmin and has lived all his life at Wadeye (Port Keats) and he has been painting for his clan group for many years. During the dry season, Maxie moves to Perrederr with his family for the bush holiday. When living at Perrederr he is hunting, looking for fresh water turtles and picking some bush tucker. The illustrations in A-Ngarryi Yagatiya contain elements from two of Maxie’s paintings about a-ngarryi yagatiya. The original art works are currently housed in the Kanamkek-Yile Ngala museum at Wadeye.

@graph.biography:
Mark Crocombe has lived and worked at Wadeye for 35 years. Originally he was as a lay missionary employ by Pat Dodson and Fr Malcolm Fyfe to assist with taking people back to their country. Later the new community council Kardu Numida employed him and he has also been self-employed working with Elders in a community fishing business. It was during this period working with Elders that his interest in natural history, cultural stories and country was reignited and he began his journey of working in cultural preservation.  

In the mid 1980s Mark started working with researchers such as Les Hiddens and others to document bush tucker and bush medicine. As part of his cultural preservation work Mark undertook to document rock art of the region which he learnt as a young man travelling though central Queensland with his father. 

Mark has been the Cultural Coordinator at Kanamkek-Yile Ngala Museum and Wadeye Aboriginal Languages Centre for a number of years, assisting in coordination documentation of languages and cultural knowledge. Today Mark is focused on digitisation of the Wadeye archives to ensure the preservation of video, audio, images and print resources. He has also become an expert photographer over the years and his images make a significant contribution to the Wadeye collection.

@graph.biography: Thomas is originally from Tasmania. He studied linguistics in Canberra and Perth. He is interested in endangered languages, especially Aboriginal languages of the western part of the Kimberley region of Western Australia. He has worked with speakers of a number of Kimberley languages including Ngarinyin and Worrorra. Thomas helped establish Worrorra arriarrganang (Worrorra revitalization project) with a Worrorra speaker at Mowanjum community in 2009. This project worked collaboratively with Batchelor Press to produce Worrorra language materials. In 2012 this work was expanded to include the related Ngarinyin and Wunambal languages and has since then operated as the Mowanjum Endangered Languages Program. Thomas has worked as the linguist on this program together with Batchelor Institute and members of Mowanjum Community including the Mowanjum Aboriginal Art and Culture Centre. Thomas has worked as a linguist for the Kimberley Language Research Centres and as a linguistic consultant. He has worked in the areas of Native Title, collaborated with scientists recording traditional ecological knowledge, indigenous land management (e.g. Indigenous Protected Area consultation), biological research and Aboriginal painting documentation. He lives in Broome.

@graph.biography: Nganthamurri has lived at Wadeye (Port Keats) his whole life and is married with five children. He enjoys painting and coaching the Wudipuli Dockers football team in the wet season. Nganthamurri travels to his country at Wudipuli for hunting and to teach his children about their country. The illustrations in Muli Kanybubi Tjitjuk Kawuny Na Yagatiya contain elements from two of Nganthamurri’s paintings about Muli Kanbubi Tjitjuk Kawuny. The paintings are currently housed in Kanamkek-Yile Ngala museum at Wadeye.

@graph.biography: Palibu was born at Palibu near Kuy and his early days were spent living with his family in their country. Palibu's father Parrmiri taught him fishing and his uncle Wilhi taught him how to hunt by himnself. Palibu was the youngest of eight children. He had five older sisters and two older brothers. In 1938 Palibu's family moved from Yederr to Werntek Nganinyi (OLd MIssion) where there were 700 Aboriginal people living together. Everyone at the mission worked clearing the jungle, planting gardens or building. In 1937 Palibu's family moved to Wadeye (Port Keats) where he worked as a timer cutter on teh bandsaw. Later he was a community health worker. During this period Palibu went on many long walking journeys to Daly River. He talked to Malak Malak, Wadjiginy and Tjemerri people, to tell them to love one another. He is known as 'The Peace Maker'. Palibu also travelled widely for ceremonies, dancing Wangga and later playing the didgeridoo. In 1942 he began work at Auvern Station as a stockman. He continued working there until he became sick with malaria in 1942, an was flown to Katherine Hospital. For his work at the staion he was given 1000 pounds in wages. From Katherine he took the train to Darwin. After a few days he was flown back to Wadeye on the medical plane. After that illness, Palibu regularly walked to Daly River and back to Wadeye, carrying material and bamboo spears for his parents. Palibu was away from the community for a long time for medical treatment. When he returned to the community he had a few weeks holiday and started work. He looked after the children in the dormitories and worked int eh Wadeye shop as a book-keeper for three years. He was then advised to finish work and go on the pension. In 1989 Palibu moved back to his homeland at Kuy to live with his wife and their children and his brother Gabriel Kungul and his family. The families had few resources. They contributed half of their pension to get solar power at their outstation. Palibu and his wife Mona live at Kuy for many years taking care of younger family members. Palibu advised the Wadeye community on issues of juvenile justice and caring for younger people when he was a member of the Thamarrurr Regional Council. He worked tirelessly to record and document his langauge and culture for his children, grandchildren and the generations to come.

@graph.biography:
Alitj Ambrose Piyalam is also known as Purlda in his community. Pulda was his father’s brother’s name. Purlda was born at Ngindjirridi. He had a Marri Ngarr mother and father but he was brought up and taught Wangga by his uncle Munggum who was a famous Marri Tjevin song man. After his father died at Daly River, Purlda went to live with his uncle Ned Berida at Nadirri.

 

Purlda remembers dancing at Old Mission as a 12 year old. He quickly became famous as a dancer, performing Wangga, Lirrga, Malkarrin, Dharnpa, Wurlthirri (the song and dance genres of the Wadeye, Daly River region). He has danced at ceremonies at Palumpa, Peppiminarti, Daly River, Belyuen, and as far afield as Maningrida, Goulburn Island, Croker Island, Yarralin, Timber Creek, Kununurra, Turkey Creek and Fitzroy Crossing.

 

Purlda is famous for composing the Walakandha Wangga a-sjinmel, ‘Seagull Wangga’. Purlda worked in Father Docherty’s sawmill, build cattle yards and worked in the garden at Port Keats. Purlda worked as a senior language advisor not only in his own language but also assisting with Marri Tjevin.

@graph.biography:
Atu was born at Tjindi at Na Vebel. When he was a young teenager he left his parents at Perrederr and walked to Tjindi to stay with his auntie Kuwakwu Maggie Timber and his uncles Ditjpil and Gumbuduk. He was living in the bush learning from his family, travelling around his country. Father Docherty came to visit the family at Tjindi and asked them to move into the mission. The whole family walked away from Tjindi, all of the Rak Tulh mob. They went to Wadeye (Port Keats) when Atu was about 12 years old. He went to school at Port Keats. They used slate and chalk to write, but Atu didn’t learn much about reading and writing English because he was thinking about his country. Atu ran away from Port Keats school. Twice he went back to his country. The third time he went to Tipperary where he was working with old men from Peppimenarti. Atu also worked at Litchfield and Finnis River stations as a stockman. Then he married Rosie Bengat Gaden, at Knucky’s Lagoon before Cyclone Tracy. After Cyclone Tracy the family went to Port Keats and lived at Perrederr, Nadirri and Tjindi, going fishing and living off the country. Later they moved back to Knucky's Lagoon for medical attention for Atu’s wife. After his death, his wife Rosie and the family moved back to Wadeye. 

Atu was famous for his dancing of Wangga, Lirrga and Thanpa. He traveled all round the country, Tjindi, Nadirri, Perrederr and Wadeye. He  also travelled to Gunbalanya, Warruwi, Belyuen, Kununarra, Derby, Kalumburu, Timber Creek and Balgo taking the young men for ceremonies. He was the businessman for those ceremonies because he was Ma Narrambu-leader for the ceremonies. 

Atu was famous for teaching the ceremonies, culture, stories and language for Ma Thanggurral. In Ma Thanggurral there are two clans Lhambu Tjendi comprising the Dumoo and Kundjil families; and Lhambu Brinkin, consisting of the Mullumbuk, Kanggiyang and Berida families. 

Atu has also been an advisor for the Northern Land Council, an interpreter for the Supreme Court and a senior consultant for the mining industry.

@graph.biography:
Kampawerr Patricia Karui (nee Walanh) was born and grew up on the Mardanungamme estate. As a baby, her mother Arna carried her wrapped up in paper-bark. In about 1932, Kampawerr’s family was camped at Purnpurn, when two policemen and a tracker came looking for the famous warrior Nemarluk. The police took Kampawerr’s father, Walanh from the family, although he was innocent of the crime he was blamed for. Because the police took most of the men from Mardanungamme, all the families had to move and nobody was left living on the Mardanungamme estate. Kampawerr’s family moved to Auvergne Station after her father and uncles were taken away by the police.

When the Japanese bombed Darwin in 1942, all the prisoners were released from jail and they walked back to Port Keats Mission (Wadeye). Then Kampawerr’s father and others walked to Auvergne Station to reunite with their families. The family then walked to Port Keats Mission. When they got to the Mission, Father Richard Docherty came to their camp and talked to Kampawerr’s parents about her living in the dormitory with other young girls who were being looked after by the nuns. Kampawerr was lonely and homesick in the dormitory so she ran back home, but Father Docherty came to her camp and took her back to the convent. On Saturdays the girls’ parents came to visit and on Sundays Father Docherty would take them to the beach, or sometimes the girls would walk to Yawu or Kumewath. 

Kampawerr married Karui Thomas Karui and they had ten children. Today, Kampawerr works with the Wadeye Aboriginal Languages Centre telling stories about her country, the dreamings and taking family members to their country to teach them about their ancestry and country.

@graph.biography: Tjakul was born at Tjindi on the Moyle River. Tjakul’s grandfather was Niwilhi Charlie Brinken Barbi who was a famous painter and songman. Tjakul was a young child when he came to live at Wadeye (Port Keats). During his working life he travelled the country and had many occupations including stockman, timberman, crocodile shooter, deckhand on the Margaret Mary, and he also worked at the Royal Australia Air Force base in Darwin. Tjakul was well known for making spears for old people and his singing and dancing for ceremonies.

Tjerrwurdi Mary Jongmin (Pulda) was born at Tjerrwurdi but lived at Kungarlbarl. She was promised to Bob Jongmin and she went with him to Daly River where she was crocodile shooting.

Tjerrwurdi travelled to many places crocodile shooting with her husband and his other wives, Jeannie, Maggie and Josephine. After many years they went to Palumpa and then to Kulchil. Finally, the family went to Port Keats where Tjerrwurdi lived for the rest of her life.

Tjinbili Anthony Nemarluk was born at Wadeye. He worked as a health worker for some time before moving to the housing industry in repairs and maintenance. Tjinbili is a family man, minding his children while his wife Miriam is teaching at the school. He has been working part-time for Wadeye Aboriginal Language Centre. Tjinbili studied environmental health with Batchelor College and completed a Certificate in Environmental Health.

On completion of his studies he decided to concentrate on painting his dreams. Tjinbili’s pantings have been sent to America, Sydney and Melbourne.

When he returned to Port Keats he married and worked as a gardener until moving to the outstation at Nadirri. Much later he started his own outstation at his homeland Tjindi.

@graph.biography:
Donna has worked in a range of jobs, including teacher, teacher-linguist, graphic designer, newspaper journalist, technical writer and real estate agent.

In the 1980s she lived and taught in Arhnemland at Galiwin’ku and Warruwi, at a time when it was possible to experience the full richness of traditional Aboriginal cultures and languages before they quickly began to disappear. In the 1990s she moved to Batchelor Institute where she worked as regional lecturer, training Indigenous teachers in the Barkley Region and later in North West and North East Arnhemland.

She became involved with the endangered language project between 2002 -2004 after transferring to the Institute’s Curriculum and Research Unit (CARU). Working with Maree Klesh (Project Manager), Elizabeth Ford (Linguist) and Wadeye elders, Donna illustrated the first four books in the Dreamtime series: Mermaid Dreaming, Hairy Cheeky Yam, Emu Dreaming and Crocodile Dreaming. These books are now part of the CALL collection and serve as a permanent record of the sacred stories passed down by elders in the endangered languages of Marri Ngarr and Marri Amu. Donna now lives in the Cairns area and continues to work as a teacher and graphic designer.

@graph.biography:
Aputh was born at Wadeye and went to school at Wadeye before attending Kormilda College. When he first started at Kormilda he went with Leon Melpi, Gordon Chula, Timmy Dumoo, Alfonso Kungul and Luke Bunduck. He finished Yr 12 at Wadeye.

 

His first job was as a hygiene worker for Wadeye Council and then he went to the Guisell Centre and studied construction and building for six months. He also learnt about plumbing, pottery and other trade skills. On completion of this course he became a construction worker for Wadeye Council.

 

From Council work he moved to the school and became part of the Literature Production Centre (LPC) team where he had his first taste of producing illustrations for Murrinh Patha books.

 

After he married he moved to the Wadeye clinic , but in 1983 he went back to the LPC in the old demountable at the school. The new LPC team was Aputh, Mempi Bede Lantjin, Dittin Alo Kungul, Pinpirrith Majella Chula, Mirkun Miriam Nemerluk (Bunduck), Mayirri Damien Tunmuck and Sr Tess Ward. In those days all the books were produced in black and white off a gestetner machine. It was operated by Mayirri who was often covered in ink from the tips of his fingers to his elbows.

 

Aputh, Mayerri and Bruce Tchinburrurr went to study printing and language studies at Batchelor College, and learned how to use an offset printer. The first colour book produced by the LPC was Ku Kananturturt (1985 ), with the then LPC manager Alan Karslake. It was a story about a little gecko.

 

Aputh continued to make Murrinh Patha language resources until 2001. He decided to go out bush and live on his Country to help look after the petrol sniffers and get them on the road to recovery. He had up to 30 young men at a time and worked with them to reconnect with culture and Country. The young men would stay on the outstation for 12 months at a time and this continued until Opal fuel was introduced to Wadeye.

 

Aputh went back to work at the school, and from 2002-2007 he taught language to junior primary students; and did interpreting and translating for the non-Indigenous teachers.

 

Before retirement he took the position of Chairperson for the TRAACS Organisation at Wadeye and was also a Community Advisor. Aputh is now retired and lives on his Country for the dry season. His main goal is to spend time with his grandchildren on the weekends, teaching them about their culture, Country, hunting and fishing, and making sure they keep their language and culture strong.

@graph.biography: Djalarra Stanley Rankin works in the Lurra Language and Culture team at Maningrida College. His father's language is Djinang and his mother's language is Wurlaki, both languages belonging to country east of Maningrida. Stanley is part of the Marrangu people who share a songline that stretches from Ritjarrngu country on the Gulf of Carpentaria right up towards the mouth of the Blyth River. Stanley is a ceremonial leader of the Wurrkiganydjarr clan group and performs the songs that are part of this story in ceremonies throughout the Maningrida region.

@graph.biography: Sally Wiynmarr was born at Willeroo Station – in Wardaman it is called Muymuy – and grew up there. As a young girl she also lived at other stations where her mother and father and many other Wardaman people lived – Delamere and Manbulloo. She spent some years at Amanbidji with her husband raising a family, and now lives with some of her children and grandchildren, and other relatives, at Binjari.

@graph.biography: Bill Harney Jr is the illustrator for the book Bornorron Warrag (Batchelor Institute Press, 2023). The book's author Sally Wynmarr is his aunt (sister to Bill Harney senior). Born (1971) in Darwin, Bill Harney Jr grew up in Katherine and from the 1990s has lived mainly at Menngen (Innesvale Station) and at Binjari Community near Katherine. He has done fencing and stock work, and has a talent for drawing. He is Wardaman on his father’s and Aunt Sally’s side and Dagoman and Yangman on his mother’s and mother’s mother’s side.

This little Frilled-Necked Lizard is lying in the grass in the sun to sun himself, and he's lying on the log.

Not far from where the little Frilled-Necked Lizard is lying is the eagle sitting on the tree and watching that little lizard. But the mother of the little lizard is already watching the eagle.
And the eagle is saying to himself, 'Aa, I might have to eat that little lizard.'
Then the eagle comes down and tries to scratch the little lizar but his mother gets up really angry.
Then the little lizard is still asleep and the eagle tries to scratch her baby but the morther of the lizard fights back.
And the eagle gives up and the mother is laughing at him.

name: MPATHA_2001_786_cover.jpg
@graph.description:
A story about camping out bush and hunting. 
Free translation: 
1	This story was told to me, from my mother

2 & 3  	From the beginning this place, there were people walking around everywhere like butcher bird, blue tongue lizard and the frog.  At first they were people

4 & 5  	Then the butcherbird and the crow went together to look around for sugar bag.  They went up the hill top.  The crow said to him “I’ve found a sugar” up in the eucalyptus tree, then the butcher bird said, my brother-in-law found a sugar bag

6 & 7  	And the frog came along and said to them.  “Hey you two, can you give me some of you sugar bag please?”  And they answered him we’ve got nothing, because they told him a lie.  And the frog said to them alright then and he kept walking and he said to himself they told me a lie and they said to one another he might finished the sugar bag 

8 & 9 	He went back walking along and got to the billabong.  He said, “Why didn’t they give some of their sugar bag?”  “oh well, said the frog.  Then the frog went down to where the water was.  The frog began to drink the water, until the water was gone.  When he drank all the water, he went up and sat on top up the hill

10 & 11 	Then the crow and the butcherbird got really thirsty.  They ran all along to drink some water.  When they got there they didn’t make a sound flash, but they only walked around and noises of all dead grass.  They started digging for water.  The dirt was all dried.

12 & 13 	Then the frog called out to them, they looked around and they looked up, there he his and he looks fat sitting on top of the rock.  Then they started calling the others, the crow called when he heard them and the butcherbird called but he didn’t listen.  There were everyone had been hunting, they heard him calling to others, he told them that the frog drank all the water. They told them there’s no water left.
@graph.admin_notes: Permission - Gabriel Thardim, Marie Thardim, Therese Nermaluk

2.	Sometime he use to go down and eat, after that he would go up and fly again.

4.	When he was asleep, the old man was looking for something to eat then he saw the bird asleep.
5.	The old man, jump up and chase the bird, he caught it but it was only wing.  The bird ran off.

@graph.description: A story of a man drinking with his friends and the consequences that follow. Originally an electronic story, there is a photocopy also kept in the CALL Collection.
@graph.admin_notes:
20180703 BK - A photocopy of the book is with it in the sleeve. There are two versions of this story.  The other is 2014/2018 60/4 2/22. 
Contact Michael Jones, Kevin Morrison for consent and advice.
Contact through CLC Tennant Creek. 

Provenance sheet notes: This one is unique and valuable story. No actual title. Story starts with Alaparra yarnkakurru murru ngarra ...This copy was previously available online. (notes by SDisbray, S&R 2014, provenance sheet


Margaret Carew provided electronic version. KM delete that file (2018/139), as it is uploaded here.


 	Story about a young man who comes into town and spends his money on drinks for his mates. While they are drunk, someone else steals their food. When they wake up, they have no food or money. The man who came into town with the money is left all alone, the others leave him. He is hungry, and ends up stealing food, because no one will look after him. Now he is in jail, how will he learn his language there?

@graph.subtitle: A Murrinhpatha health dictionary
@graph.description: This community friendly health dictionary covers body parts, face parts, internal organs, hand and foot features, the skeleton and muscles. Accompanying the diagrams are introductory Murrinhpatha conversations for community nurses and patients that assist with assessing basic health issues. To assist non Murrinhpatha speakers, a pronunciation guide and brief of the Murrinhpatha language has been included. This valuable health resource has been developed by Wadeye community members for their clinic and is accompanied by five detailed posters; body parts, the skeleton, the head, internal organs and hand and foot. The book and posters are in Murrinhpatha and English. This is a valuable resource suitable for anyone involved with community health; the community clinic, aged care, child care, primary school, high school and tertiary education.

@graph.name: Songs from North Queensland
@graph.description:
12" LP record with companion booklet. Recordings of songs in various languages, with notes on the music and performances, song words, phonetics, musical notes and tape catalogue details. 

CAUTION NOTE on the record: 'Discretion should be exercised in playing these recorded songs in the presence of Aboriginal people. The recorded voices of singers now deceased may cause distress to listening relatives. In the case of exclusive men's and women's songs, it is advisable to ensure that these are not played to mixed Aboriginal audiences or in the presence of Aboriginal children. Moreover, it will be appreciated that certain ritual songs may mean more to some Aboriginal groups than others. As a general principle, in any one Aboriginal community, recorded songs should be played first to a group of older Aboriginal people. Permission might then be sought from these people before further playback to others.'

Mark Crocombe (who made the recording) was also present.

N.B.: 
numerous recordings of this word list exist with different speakers and in the different languages of Murrinhpatha, Marri Amu, Marri Tjevin, Marri Ngarr.

Mark Crocombe at start states that the word list is Marri Amu and Marri Tjevin, however it seems to be only Marri Tjevin (after word in English)??
Was this Marri Tjevin list recorded over a previous one that had the two languages (?)
[KM contacted MC by email 24.11.2023]
KM to follow up
[Notes by KM 24 Nov 2023]
